intro: You are looking for a private dentist to fit a crown, and you want to find the best one near you. A crown is a significant investment, so it is worth understanding what 'best' means for your tooth and how to compare your local options.
need_heading: What people searching for a private crown near them usually need
need_lead: Most people want a crown that looks natural, fits comfortably and lasts, from a dentist they can reach easily.
needs: You have a damaged or heavily filled tooth and your dentist has advised a crown to protect it.
You want a crown that matches your other teeth in colour and shape, especially if it is near the front.
You are considering a private crown because you want a wider choice of materials or a particular type of ceramic.
You need to know the full cost before you commit, including any lab fees or follow-up appointments.
You want to find a dentist close to home or work so that appointments and any adjustments are convenient.
context_heading: How to judge which private crown is best for you
context: There is no single 'best' crown or dentist, because the right choice depends on your tooth, your bite and what you want from the crown. Private dentistry lets you and your dentist discuss materials such as metal-ceramic or all-ceramic, and the lab that will make it, so you can weigh up appearance, strength and cost.

When comparing dentists, ask about their experience with the type of crown you need and how they match the shade to your other teeth. You can check that any dentist you see is registered with the General Dental Council (GDC) on their online register, and in England you can check whether the practice is registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC).
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Which tooth needs the crown and whether it is visible when you smile.
Whether your dentist has already recommended a particular type of crown or material.
Any concerns you have about the appearance of the crown, such as shade matching.
Your rough location and how far you are willing to travel for appointments.
Whether you have a deadline, such as a wedding or holiday, for having the crown fitted.
Any previous experience of dental treatment that you would like the dentist to know about.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the private dentist
questions: Which dental lab will make my crown, and can you tell me about the materials they use?
How will you make sure the crown matches the shade of my other teeth?
What is the full cost of the crown, including any appointments before and after fitting?
How long should the crown last, and what can I do to look after it?
What happens if the crown feels uncomfortable or breaks?
Can you show me examples of crowns you have fitted for similar teeth?

faqs.q: How do I find the best private dentist for a crown near me?
faqs.a: Start by checking that the dentist is registered with the General Dental Council (GDC), and in England that the practice is registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC). Then ask about their experience with the type of crown you need and whether they can explain the material and lab choices clearly.

faqs.q: Is a private crown better than an NHS one?
faqs.a: Private crowns offer a wider choice of materials and labs, including highly aesthetic ceramics, but 'better' depends on your tooth and your priorities. Discuss the options with your dentist so you can weigh up appearance, strength and cost.

faqs.q: What should I do if I have a problem with a private crown?
faqs.a: First speak to the practice where you had the crown fitted and follow their complaints process. If the issue is not resolved, the Dental Complaints Service can help with private dental complaints.

faqs.q: Can I check if a dentist is qualified to fit crowns?
faqs.a: Yes, all dentists must be registered with the General Dental Council (GDC), and you can check the register online. If the dentist uses a specialist title, such as prosthodontist, they must also be on a GDC specialist list.

extra_heading: What to expect at a crown consultation
extra: A first appointment for a crown is usually about assessment rather than treatment. The dentist will look at the tooth, may take an X-ray to check the root and surrounding bone, and will talk through whether a crown is the right way to protect it. This is your chance to ask about materials and see shade guides against your own teeth.

If you go ahead, the tooth is usually prepared and a temporary crown fitted while the permanent one is made at a dental lab. The fit and bite are checked when it is cemented, and a review appointment lets the dentist adjust anything that feels high or rough. Ask in advance how many visits this will take so you can plan around work or caring commitments.

Because 'near me' matters for crowns, think about how easy it is to get back to the practice if the crown feels uncomfortable after fitting. A dentist slightly further away who explains things clearly may suit you better than the closest one, and that is a judgement only you can make once you have spoken to them.

extra_faqs.q: Will I need X-rays before a crown?
extra_faqs.a: Often yes, because the dentist needs to see the health of the root and the bone around the tooth before deciding on a crown. Ask whether any X-ray charge is included in the quote you receive.

extra_faqs.q: Can I choose the colour of my crown?
extra_faqs.a: You can discuss shade with your dentist, and they will usually match it to your neighbouring teeth rather than to the brightest white. If the tooth is near the front, ask to see the shade in different lighting before it is finalised.

extra_faqs.q: What if the crown feels wrong once it is fitted?
extra_faqs.a: Tell the practice promptly so they can check the bite and adjust or remake it if needed. If you are not satisfied after their complaints process, the Dental Complaints Service can help with private dental complaints.
